# Setup

### These libraries are used for the locator map

```{r}
library(sf)
```

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
library(rnaturalearth)
```

```{r}
library(rnaturalearthdata)
```

```{r}

```

```{r}
library(rnaturalearthhires)
```

```{r}
library(devtools)
```

### These are the data for the locator map

```{r}
states <- (ne_states(country = "United States of America"))
```

```{r}
lakes50 <- ne_download(
  scale = 50, 
  type = "lakes", 
  category = "physical")
```

```{r}
rivers50 <- ne_download(
  scale = 50,
  type = "rivers_lake_centerlines",
  category = "physical",
  returnclass = "sf"
)
```

```{r}
utah <- states %>%
  filter(name == "Utah")
```

### This is the code chunk to produce the locator map

```{r}
ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = world, fill = "lightgray") +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = lakes50, fill = "blue", color = "lightblue") +
  geom_sf(data = utah, fill = "antiquewhite1", color = "green")+
    geom_text(data = states, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, label = name), size = 3.0, fontface = "bold", nudge_y = states$nudge_y) +
    geom_sf(data = rivers50, color = "lightblue", size = 0.2) +
    coord_sf(xlim = c(-125, -100), ylim = c(30, 50), expand = FALSE) +
    ggtitle("Western United States", subtitle = "with a focus on Utah")+
    theme_void()
```

### These are the libraries used for the ski resort map

```{r}
library(osmdata)
```

```{r}
library(leaflet)
```

### This is the Open Street Map data for Ski Resorts within a Western US bounding box

```{r}
skiresorts <- opq (bbox = c (-125, 30, -100, 50)) %>% 
    add_osm_feature (key = "landuse", value = "winter_sports", value_exact = FALSE) %>%
    osmdata_sf ()
```

### This is the code chunk to produce the ski resort map

```{r}
leaflet() %>%
  addTiles() %>%
  addPolygons(
    data = skiresorts$osm_polygons,
    label = skiresorts$osm_polygons$name
  ) 
```

### This is the additional library used for the palms map

```{r}
library(rinat)
```

### This is the iNaturalist observations of palms in the Western US

```{r}
inat_palms_obs_df <- get_inat_obs(taxon_id = 50184, place_id = 1, quality = "research", geo = TRUE, maxresults = 2000)
```

```{r}
save(inat_palms_obs_df, file = "USA_Palms_inat.Rdata")
```

```{r}
inat_palms_obs_sf <-  inat_palms_obs_df %>% 
  select(longitude, latitude, datetime, common_name, scientific_name, image_url, user_login) %>% 
  st_as_sf(coords=c("longitude", "latitude"), crs=4326)
```

```{r}
dim(inat_palms_obs_sf)
```

```{r}
inat_palms_obs_popup_sf <- inat_palms_obs_sf %>% 
  mutate(popup_html = paste0("<p><b>", common_name, "</b><br/>",
                             "<i>", scientific_name, "</i></p>",
                             "<p>Observed: ", datetime, "<br/>",
                             "User: ", user_login, "</p>",
                             "<p><img src='", image_url, "' style='width:100%;'/></p>"))
```

### This is the code chunk used to produce the palms map

```{r}
leaflet(inat_palms_obs_sf) %>% 
  setView(lng = -112, lat = 40, zoom = 5)%>%
  addTiles() %>% 
  addCircleMarkers(data = inat_palms_obs_popup_sf,
                   popup = ~popup_html, 
                   radius = 5)
```

### This is the code chunk used to produce the "Palms in Proximity to Ski Resorts" map

```{r}
palmskimap <- leaflet(inat_palms_obs_sf) %>% 
  setView(lng = -112, lat = 37, zoom = 5)%>%
  addTiles() %>% 
  addCircleMarkers(data = inat_palms_obs_popup_sf,
                   popup = ~popup_html, color = "darkorange",
                   radius = 1) %>%
  addTiles() %>%
  addPolygons(data = skiresorts$osm_polygons,
    label = skiresorts$osm_polygons$name)
m <- palmskimap %>%
  addLegend(position = "topright", colors = c("darkorange", "blue"), labels = c("Fan Palms", "Ski Resorts"))
```

# Introduction

My project will focus on the Western United States. I am Jake Flanigan, and I am in Salt Lake City, UT. My grandfather was a National Parks wildlife bioligist, so my mom was raised in several national parks across the Western US. And with all her background she touts that her current living situation is one of the best in world: "Where else can you travel 2 hours and change temperature this much?" Between Beaver, UT and Mesquite, NV there is often a 15F difference in temperature. Locals in Southern Utah say, "You can ski one day and waterski the next." My topics will attempt to find where else, if anywhere, there are others places where people can quickly and conveniently migrate to warmth for the winter.

We will keep a close eye on Utah while we attempt to visualize where climate differences are in close proximity.

```{r}
ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = world, fill = "lightgray") +
  geom_sf(data = states, fill = "white") +
  geom_sf(data = lakes50, fill = "blue", color = "lightblue") +
  geom_sf(data = utah, fill = "antiquewhite1", color = "green")+
    geom_text(data = states, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, label = name), size = 3.0, fontface = "bold", nudge_y = states$nudge_y) +
    geom_sf(data = rivers50, color = "lightblue", size = 0.2) +
    coord_sf(xlim = c(-125, -100), ylim = c(30, 50), expand = FALSE) +
    ggtitle("Western United States", subtitle = "with a focus on Utah")+
    theme_void()
```

# Cool summer life in the accessible mountainous areas of the West.

The locations of ski resorts will be used to define areas where people could recreate outdoors comfortably in the summer but are likely to migrate to warmer weather for the winter. I'm satisfied with this variable although it is not directly related to specific climates or seasonal temperature ranges. Since my question is not only about temperature difference, but also about where populations of people exist that would seasonally migrate, ski resorts should be a good variable to visualize summer living locations. The map below shows the location of ski resorts across the Western United States, hover over a location marked by a blue dot and the name of the ski area will appear.

```{r}
leaflet() %>%
  addTiles() %>%
  addPolygons(
    data = skiresorts$osm_polygons,
    label = skiresorts$osm_polygons$name
  ) 
```

# Warm winter life in coastal and developed inland areas of the Western US

The presence of palm trees will be used to define areas where people are likely to escape during the winter. To draw on memories of the area from where this question originates, the town of St. George, Utah wraps the core of all its palm trees along the main boulevard to keep them from the few freezing nights in the winters. Since it is the furthest north "retirement town" on Interstate 15, I think the presence of palms sufficiently represents areas that people move to for the winter. It also conveniently marks where people live since we tend to use them in landscaping where they are able to survive. Since there are many palm species, I'm going to narrow my query to California Fan Palms, because that is the species in Utah that has observations on the iNaturalist website.

```{r}
leaflet(inat_palms_obs_sf) %>% 
  setView(lng = -112, lat = 37, zoom = 5)%>%
  addTiles() %>% 
  addCircleMarkers(data = inat_palms_obs_popup_sf,
                   popup = ~popup_html, color = "darkorange",
                   radius = 2)
```

# Sustainability and Mapping Proximity of Cool Summer and Warm Winter Destinations

Identifying areas in the Western US where cool summer and warm winter climates are in close proximity could be useful to coarsley inform quite a few Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of the United Nations. Goals 1 and 2 are to end poverty and hunger, and there is an apparent and possibly substantial amount of impoverished homeless people that migrate between cool summer and warm winter climates. These data could help identify areas where migrating homeless may be in need of nutrition services or other attention. Good health and education goals could be targeted to where people are likely to live seasonally in two homes. This may be becoming more common as more people are able to live in two homes annually as wealth builds and remote working continues to expand. This leads me to ideas of how it may be used in economic growth and infrastructure described in SDGs 8 & 9. My analyses and this project will mostly focus on goals 11 & 12, "sustainable cities & communities" and "responsible consumption and production"

Source: <https://sdgs.un.org/goals>![](images/SDGs 1-12.png)

# Map Interpretation

These interactive maps above show where California fan palms have been observed in orange and locations of ski resorts in blue. These locations represent populated (except coastlines where palms grow naturally) areas where people are likely to seasonally migrate from cool summer climates to warm or, at least, fair weather for the winter. The locations of ski resorts were sourced from Open Street Map and the observations of California fan palms were sourced from iNaturalist. Noticing that there are no palm trees near the California border and only observed further south in other states, we can focus and zoom slightly into the Southwest US. With this visualization, its clearly apparent that there are several areas in the southwest where ski resorts are found in relatively close proximity. Since our exploration started in Southern Utah, the distance between the furthest south ski resort in Utah and the furthest north palm in Utah can be visually compared to the distance between other populated cool summer and warm winter areas. Are there areas where ski resorts and palms are found as close or closer than in Southern Utah? If the map is observed clockwise from St. George, UT, we can see that there are no areas with mild winters to the north nor east. To the SSE, Arizona Snow Bowl near Flagstaff, AZ and scenic Sedona, AZ are found in slightly closer proximity. There's even a small ski resort found near Las Vegas, NV. In Southern California, Big Bear Ski Resort and a couple of others are very near to very mild and populated cities such as Riverside, Lancaster, and Santa Clarita. Even Los Angeles and its suburbs compare in to Southern Utah's ski and palm proximity. Further north along the Sierra Mts we can see that Fresno, Stockton, and Sacramento all with mild winters, are close to several ski resorts and cool mountain summer air. This map makes it clear that there are several places besides Southern Utah where people can travel fairly short distances while seasonally migrating for fair weather. So, although it's not unique to Southern Utah it is unique to the southwest portion of the US, and most common in California.

# Recommendations

Educating the public about these locations can help make choices that conserve money and resource while still enjoying the comforts and benefits of seasonal migration. Furthermore, as heat waves become more common, developed areas like ski resorts where people could escape heat waves without traveling far may be beneficial to identify. The shorter ranges of electric vehicles may make this information more relevant to people buying their first electric vehicle. If a person wanted to continue outdoor recreation or without the discomfort of freezing or hot temperatures or just avoid the cold to avoid arthritic pain but not have suffer the sweltering heat of summers, or any other reason the flocks of retired "snowbirds" travel south for the winter, they could make a choice between commuting between Alberta, Canada and Southern Texas or any of the areas that are closer on this map. Assuming, they traveled once between winter and summer homes, there would be far fewer resources consumed over shorter migrations. This is just one more way that our educated and technological society can make choices that move us toward our Sustainable Development Goals.

# Limitations and Ideas for Improvement

There are many limitations of using the two variables of locations of ski resorts and presence of California fan palms to answer the question of where Western Americans may be able to migrate seasonally while minimizing resource use. It could be assumed that migrating to fair weather would use less energy on heating and cooling, but that could depend on factors of human behavior like if the summer home was "winterized" and energy consumption was minimized while gone. If water heaters, HVAC sytems, or any powered devices are left on while simultaneously using energy at a second home, there may be far more consumption than potential energy savings. Similarly, if people move back and forth between their two homes more often when it is close and convenient, they may consume comparable amounts or even more energy than someone flying long distances between homes once per season. Besides these complex limitations of modeling human behavior, there is the more obvious limitation of conveniently available data like fan palms observations being an accurate model of a nice place to live in the winters. I actually have more confidence that fan palms represent a winter escape than ski resorts represent areas where people will immigrate for summers and emigrate for winters. I predict there are far more cold areas that retirees commonly escape from in the winter that are not in proximity to ski resorts, and therefore not well represented. Diving deeper into available seasonal temperature data and researching where people tend to migrate seasonally could add accuracy to this visualization and would likely identify even more areas where one could travel a short distance to experience favorable temperature. The distance between two living areas may also be less important to people's choices and energy savings than the time, traffic conditions, miles of road, safety, etc. Using a travel times calculator like was mentioned in our course's Slack channel would be interesting to apply to the handful of areas highlighted as close seasonal migration possibliites in the Interpretation section. I'd guess, and have heard, it's sometimes feels more convenient to fly to Salt Lake City to ski than drive from LA to Big Bear Ski Resort because of traffic and accommodation hassles.

Thanks to Open Street Map and iNaturalist for the data to create this project. My family and friends in Southern Utah may not like hearing that California has the likeliest chance for sustainable seasonal migration, but facts are facts :)
